This course teaches Dr. Bardia Khosravani’s FIS method: buy shares of companies that make real profit and pay a good part of it to shareholders as cash dividends.
The “In Dr. Khosravani’s words” boxes are his exact sentences, with their source.
Like class notes written from a professor’s book: the book is his, but someone else wrote the notes.
FIS: Real Profit, Not Charts
FIS stands for Fundamental Investing System.
Its main question is: how much money does this company make, and what is it worth?
Its data comes from Codal, the official website for listed companies’ reports.
Buying a share is like becoming a partner in a bakery. FIS reads the bakery’s books of income and expenses.
Why Fundamental, Not Technical?
Technical analysis uses the price and volume chart to guess which way the price will go.
On the Tehran exchange, price limits, trading halts and rumours from Telegram channels make the chart noisy.
But the company’s real profit is recorded on Codal every month, and in the long run the price follows profit.
The FIS horizon is 1 to 5 years. Its main risks are misjudging profit and having to wait a long time.
To buy a shop, you read its monthly sales book, not how busy the door looks on one day.
FLM: Managing Yourself
FLM is the other side of the coin: managing fear and greed, mental mistakes, and how much of your money goes where.
Good analysis with bad behaviour earns nothing. Someone who sells at the bottom out of fear loses money even with the best analysis.
FIS says it is a good bakery; FLM makes sure you don’t sell your share cheap out of fear after one slow day.
This app is educational and is not advice to buy or sell.
No method, FIS included, gives guaranteed profit. The aim is fewer big mistakes and a better chance of a positive real return in the long run.
The companies in the examples are made up. “(check)” means you should check that detail yourself in the official source.
Dr. Khosravani himself made and endorsed this app.

Get Your Money Ready
Day-to-day spending (1 to 3 months of costs): a bank account.
Emergency fund (6 to 12 months of living costs): a fixed-income fund or a short-term deposit.
Goals 1 to 3 years away, like a home or a wedding: fixed income, Akhza or gold.
Growth capital, meaning money you won’t need for at least 5 years: stocks, using the FIS method.
You don’t buy stocks with next month’s rent; if the market falls, you would have to sell cheap to pay the rent.
Why Not Short-Term Money in Stocks?
Stocks can fall 40% or more in a single year.
If you need some money soon, a fall forces you to sell at a loss.
That is why personal readiness is the first step, before any analysis.
If you put next year’s home-buying money into stocks and the market drops 40%, either the purchase is delayed or you have to sell at a loss.

Market Players
The Securities and Exchange Organization (SEO) is the market’s referee: it sets the rules, supervises disclosure and approves capital increases.
Shares trade on the Tehran Stock Exchange and Farabourse. Farabourse’s “base market” means the company doesn’t meet the full requirements; a warning sign.
Codal is the official home of all company reports. Samat records share ownership and pays cash dividends. tsetmc shows the day’s price and volume.
Like a football match: SEO is the referee, the exchange is the pitch, Codal the official scoreboard, and tsetmc the live commentator.
Commodity Exchange: News Before Codal
Companies such as steel, petrochemical, cement and copper makers sell their products on the commodity exchange.
The price discovered there shows the company’s next-month selling price sooner than the Codal report.
If the price of rebar on the commodity exchange rose 10% this month, the steel company’s next monthly report will probably show a higher selling price.
You Can’t Always Sell
Price limit: each day the price can move only up to a set ceiling and floor (the percentage changes now and then; check).
In a crisis, sell queues form and you may not be able to sell for several days.
Trading halt: before major news, a general meeting or a capital increase, trading in the stock is stopped, sometimes for a long time.
Who Holds the Shares?
A government or holding-company major shareholder may decide in its own interest; for example, it may want high dividends for its own cash needs even when the company needs the money.
Free float is the part of the shares in public hands that actually trades. When it is small, the price can stay far from value for a long time.
If a shop’s main owner takes all the takings every month for personal spending, the shop has no money left to buy stock.
The government also has a big effect: set prices, the official exchange rate, feedstock and energy prices, taxes and export duties.

If your money grows 40% but prices rise 45%, you are poorer.
The right calculation is not simple subtraction. Example: nominal 60% and inflation 40% → 1.6 ÷ 1.4 − 1 = 14.3% (not 20%).
Last year 100 tomans bought 10 loaves of bread. This year you have 160 tomans but a loaf costs 14; you can buy about 11.4 loaves. You are only 14% richer, not 60%.
Nominal Gain, Real Loss
Nominal 40% and inflation 45%: 1.4 ÷ 1.45 − 1 = −3.4%.
A negative number means your buying power fell, even though you have more money.
Type a negative number with a minus sign.
A fund paying 25% in a year of 35% inflation has actually cut your buying power by about 7%.
A Stock Must Beat These Three
1. The risk-free rate: the return on Akhza (Islamic treasury bills) or a fixed-income fund. If a stock doesn’t pay more, you have taken its risk for nothing.
2. Inflation: at the very least, to keep your buying power.
3. What people buy instead of stocks: the dollar, gold coins and housing; money moves between them.
If Akhza pays 30% with no hassle, a stock that pays 25% with a lot of stress is a bad deal.
If a company can raise its product prices along with inflation or the dollar, its profit grows with inflation too; such a stock is called “inflation-proof”.
If the government keeps the selling price fixed while costs rise with inflation, profit melts away.
A free-market bakery sells bread for more when flour gets expensive; a bakery with a government-set price can’t, and its profit melts away.
Financial Statements Don’t Keep Up With Inflation
Machines bought cheaply years ago are still on the books at their old price.
So depreciation (the wearing out of machines) is under-counted, and profit on paper looks bigger than real profit.
That is why “book value” and the P/B ratio (price to book value) mean less in Iran.
Iran does not apply its version of the international standard IAS 29 (financial reporting in hyperinflation).
Real return is exactly “nominal return minus inflation”.
Subtraction is only an approximation, and with high inflation it is far off.

NAV means the real value of the fund’s assets per unit.

Practice Folder and Sources
Before the Codal lessons, build this folder so you can practise everything you learn on real companies.
Pick 8 to 10 companies from 4 different industries, such as cement, petrochemicals, pharmaceuticals, banking, steel and food. Each industry has its own report shape and risks.

Make a spreadsheet for each company with 4 tabs: monthly (quantity, price, sales amount), quarterly (profit and loss for each 3 months), events (capital increases, general meetings, important announcements) and a decision journal.
30 minutes each week: open the new Codal announcements and enter the numbers. Numbers first, then the price on tsetmc, so the price doesn’t colour your judgement.
Before each report comes out, forecast your own number and write it down. Forecast errors are the best teacher.
Keep a paper portfolio with written reasons for at least 3 months, and compare the result with the overall index and a fixed-income fund.
